title: Telling about the weekend
goal: Bring the whole module together in one long conversation — three tenses, subordinate clauses, comparisons, and the little words that make your sentences sound Norwegian, not translated.
bekal: switch between present, past, the *har* form and the future in one story
use *det er* and *det finnes* to say that something exists
slip in *jo*, *da*, *nok* and *vel* — little words that aren't translated but are always heard
wave: Review **unit 18** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Test one thing: where does *ikke* stand inside a subordinate clause?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — En helg på hytta
dialogs.intro: Monday morning, early October. Budi has just come back from his first weekend at Ingrid's family cabin, and he looks like someone who has experienced something he can't fully explain.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Der er du jo! Hvordan gikk helga?
lines.id: There you are! How was the weekend?
lines.literal: there are you indeed! how went weekend-the?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rart. Fint, men rart. Det fantes ikke internett.
lines.id: Strange. Nice, but strange. There was no internet.
lines.literal: strange. nice, but strange. it existed not internet.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Selvfølgelig ikke. Det er hele poenget med ei hytte.
lines.id: Of course not. That's the whole point of a cabin.
lines.literal: of-course not. that is whole point-the with a cabin.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vi kjørte i tre timer, og så gikk vi førti minutter til.
lines.id: We drove for three hours, and then walked another forty minutes.
lines.literal: we drove in three hours, and then walked we forty minutes more.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Med sekk, med mat for tre dager, og med ved. Jeg har aldri båret så mye.
lines.id: With backpacks, food for three days, and firewood. I've never carried so much.
lines.literal: with backpack, with food for three days, and with firewood. I have never carried so much.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Da var det mørkt og fire grader inne. Ingrid tente peisen med en gang.
lines.id: It was dark and four degrees inside. Ingrid lit the fireplace right away.
lines.literal: then was it dark and four degrees inside. Ingrid lit fireplace-the with one time.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Og etter en time var det varmt, og du forsto hvorfor vi gjør det.
lines.id: And after an hour it was warm, and you understood why we do it.
lines.literal: and after one hour was it warm, and you understood why we do it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg forsto det ikke med en gang. Men på søndag morgen satt jeg ute med kaffe, og da forsto jeg.
lines.id: Not right away. But on Sunday morning I sat outside with coffee, and then I understood.
lines.literal: I understood it not with one time. but on Sunday morning sat I outside with coffee, and then understood I.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Der ser du. Skal du dra igjen?
lines.id: There you go. Will you go again?
lines.literal: there see you. shall you leave again?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Til vinteren, hvis de vil ha meg med. Men da tar jeg med tykkere sokker.
lines.id: This winter, if they'll have me along. But then I'm bringing thicker socks.
lines.literal: to winter-the, if they want have me with. but then take I with thicker socks.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nesten. Jeg klager fortsatt om været.
lines.id: Almost. I still complain about the weather.
lines.literal: almost. I complain still about weather-the.

notes: **Notice how many tenses switch in one short conversation**: *gikk* (past), *er* (present), *har aldri båret* (the *har* form), *skal dra* (future). This is what real conversation demands, and it's what you have after nineteen units.
**Det fantes ikke internett** uses *å finnes* in the past tense. Compare *det var ikke internett*, which is also correct but sounds flatter. *Finnes* stresses that there really was none at all.

**Der er du jo!** — the word *jo* here can't be translated. It signals "as expected" or "you know", and leaving it out makes the sentence sound cold. This family of little words is covered on the next page.
**Da dere kom fram** uses *da* because the event is in the past and happened once — the rule from unit 18. If you use *når* here, Norwegians will understand but file it as a newcomer's mistake.
**På søndag morgen satt jeg ute** — this sentence opens with a time expression, so the verb is in second place and the subject moves back. The V2 rule from unit 3, still at work in the last unit.

**Du er blitt norsk** uses *er* as the helping verb instead of *har* — the form used for changes of state and movement. *Han er gått* (he has gone), *hun er kommet* (she has come). The form with *har* is also correct and more common; recognize both.

grammars.title: Det er, det finnes, det ligger
body: To say that something exists, Norwegian uses *det* as an empty subject — just like English "there is" or "it's raining".

head: Norsk
English
Tone
rows: There's a cabin in the woods.

after: *Det* here is **required** and can't be dropped, even though it refers to nothing. Just as English can't say "is raining", Norwegian never can either.
When the thing is already definite, the order changes and *det* disappears: *Butikken er her* (the shop is here), not *det er butikken her*.
*Det er* is also used to introduce people: *Det er Ingrid* (that's Ingrid), *Det er meg* (it's me, on the phone).

grammars.title: Little words that aren't translated
body: This is what separates correct Norwegian from Norwegian that sounds alive. They all sit in slot four, and they can all be dropped without breaking the grammar — but the sentence goes flat.
after: Don't force yourself to use them all at once. Start with two: **jo** and **nok**. They're heard most and are the safest.
⚠️ *Da* at the end of a sentence is completely different from *da* the conjunction ("when"). Position tells them apart: at the end it's emphasis, at the start of a clause it's time.
These words are why word-for-word translations from English always sound stiff. Adding one *jo* or *nok* in the right place makes you sound more fluent than ten new vocabulary words.

grammars.title: The whole tense system in one table
body: This sums up five units at once. If you can read this table from top to bottom without stopping, your A1 is complete.
after: The fourth row is the only one not covered before: *hadde* + the third form says something had already happened **before** another past event. *Da jeg kom, hadde de allerede spist* — when I arrived, they had already eaten. Just like English "had eaten".
These seven rows cover everything A1 needs and most of A2. What's left for the next level is the passive, the conditional, and a large number of phrasal verbs.

sections.title: Words that tie a story together

blocks.text: Telling a story takes linking words, not just verbs. These words turn a list of sentences into a story.

All eight fill slot one, so the verb follows right away and the subject moves back: *Så **gikk vi** hjem.* Plain joining words like *og* and *men* just link and change nothing: *…og **vi gikk** hjem.* This is the rule from unit 3, and it still applies to the last sentence you'll ever write.

You're now at **full A1**: you can introduce yourself, handle everyday needs, talk about what has happened and what will happen, and link sentences into paragraphs. What comes next isn't new grammar but **volume**.

items: **Vocabulary.** This module gave you about six hundred words. A2 takes around fifteen hundred, and B1 around three thousand. The fastest way to grow it isn't word lists but reading — start with the easy news at *klartale.no*, then *NRK Skole*.

**Listening.** This is what falls furthest behind when you learn from a book. The podcasts *Lær norsk nå* and *Norsklærer Karense* are made for learners; NRK P1 radio is made for native speakers and will feel impossible for the first few weeks. Listen to both.

**Dialects.** Once you're comfortable with Oslo speech, the next surprise is that almost nobody talks exactly like that. Norway has no standard spoken dialect, and people speak their regional dialect even on national TV. It feels unfair at first and becomes fun later.

**Exams.** If you need official proof — for university, permanent residence or citizenship — the exam is called **Norskprøven**, run by Kompetanse Norge, and it tests four separate skills. A2 is enough for many jobs; B1 is required for citizenship; B2 for most university programs.

blocks.title: Ten minutes a day
items: What matters most isn't how long you study in one sitting, but how often you come back. Ten minutes every day beats three hours every Sunday, by a wide margin.
Go through this module again from unit 1 in reverse: read the English, and rebuild the Norwegian from memory. The second round feels very different from the first.
**Lykke til.** And if you've made it to this page, you can read that without a translation.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: internett / fantes / det / ikke
timer / kjørte / tre / vi / i
mørkt / kom / da / var / fram / vi / det / ,
igjen / skal / dra / du / ?
øver / norsk / jeg / snakke / vi / kan / ? /

answers: kjørte — bor — sett — skal — hadde — kommer
Så gikk vi hjem. — Derfor var jeg trøtt. — Likevel dro vi. — Etterpå ble det varmt. — Til slutt spiste vi middag. — Endelig forsto jeg alt.
Det fantes ikke internett der. — Vi kjørte i tre timer. — Jeg har aldri båret så mye. — Da vi kom fram, var det mørkt. — Til vinteren skal jeg dra dit igjen. — Kan vi snakke norsk? Jeg øver.
Det fantes ikke internett. — Vi kjørte i tre timer. — Da vi kom fram, var det mørkt. — Skal du dra igjen? — Kan vi snakke norsk? Jeg øver.
